title: Greetings
description: Hello and goodbye across the day, with formality notes.

steps.title: A soft start
steps.body: German greetings shift with time of day and formality. Learn a small set well.

steps.title: Form vs. familiarity
steps.body: Use Sie with strangers and formal situations. Use du with friends and family when invited.
bullets: Guten Morgen in the morning.
Guten Tag during the day.
Guten Abend in the evening.
Hallo is friendly and casual.

phrases.target: Guten Tag, wie geht es Ihnen?
Mir geht’s gut, danke. Und dir?

steps.prompt: Match each German greeting with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Hello, how are you?":
steps.targetSentence: Guten Tag, wie geht es Ihnen?
steps.explanation: A warm, time-appropriate greeting — the foundation of any first impression.

steps.title: Listen · evening
steps.prompt: You hear this in the evening. What does it mean?

steps.partnerSays: Guten Tag, freut mich. Wie geht es Ihnen?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Good day, pleased to meet you. How are you?
steps.prompt: Reply politely, keeping the formal Sie:
steps.explanation: "Sehr gut, danke. Und Ihnen?" answers warmly and returns the question with the formal Ihnen.

steps.title: Check · time of day
steps.prompt: Which greeting fits the evening?
steps.explanation: Guten Abend is the evening greeting.

steps.title: Check · formality
steps.prompt: You meet your friend’s parent for the first time. Best choice?
options: Guten Tag, wie geht es Ihnen?
steps.explanation: Sie keeps things respectful.

steps.title: Check · going to sleep
steps.prompt: You’re heading to bed. You say…
steps.explanation: Gute Nacht is for going to sleep.

title: Please & thank you
description: Politeness formulas that open every exchange.

steps.title: Small words, big difference
steps.body: German interactions expect bitte and danke. Skipping them can sound abrupt.

steps.title: Please & thanks
steps.body: Bitte means both “please” and “you’re welcome.”
bullets: Vielen Dank = thank you very much.
Bitte / Gern geschehen = you’re welcome.
Entschuldigung = excuse me / sorry.
Es tut mir leid is a stronger apology.

steps.prompt: Match each German polite phrase with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "A coffee, please.":
steps.explanation: Combining a request with "please" — the cornerstone of polite interaction.

steps.title: Listen · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says Danke. A common reply is…

steps.partnerSays: Hier bitte, Ihr Kaffee. Das macht drei Euro.
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Here you go, your coffee. That's three euros.
steps.prompt: Thank him as you pay:
steps.explanation: "Vielen Dank" is the natural thank-you at this point in the exchange.

steps.title: Check · shop
steps.prompt: How do you say “please” when ordering?
steps.explanation: Bitte is the standard polite request word.

steps.title: Check · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says Danke. A common reply is…
steps.explanation: Bitte also means “you’re welcome.”

title: Numbers 1–10
description: Count clearly for prices, times, and quantities.

steps.title: Count slowly
steps.body: German numbers are used constantly. Rhythm first; speed later.

steps.title: Notes
steps.body: Eins becomes ein before masculine/neuter nouns.
bullets: ein Buch, eine Apfel
Learn numbers in short phrases.

steps.prompt: Match each German number with its numeral:
Arrange the stones to say: "Two coffees, please.":
steps.explanation: Numbers in context — the essential combination for real-world transactions.

steps.title: Listen · age
steps.prompt: Someone says this. How old are they?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: How many tickets would you like?
steps.prompt: Ask for two tickets:
steps.explanation: "Zwei Tickets, bitte" answers with a number and a polite request. "Das macht fünfzehn Euro" is what the clerk would say.

steps.title: Check · seven
steps.prompt: What is “seven” in German?
steps.explanation: Sieben is seven.

steps.title: Check · phrase
steps.prompt: “Zwei Kaffee” means…
steps.explanation: Zwei means two.

steps.title: Check · age
steps.prompt: How do Germans say “I am twenty years old”?
steps.explanation: Age uses sein + … Jahre alt.

title: Introduce yourself
description: Name, origin, and a simple nice-to-meet-you.

steps.title: First contact
steps.body: A short self-introduction is enough: name, origin, and a polite close.

steps.title: Freut mich
steps.body: Freut mich (or Es freut mich) is the standard “nice to meet you.”

steps.prompt: Match each German introduction phrase with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Hello, my name is Alex.":
steps.explanation: Your origin in one clear sentence — the natural follow-up to sharing your name.

steps.title: Listen · origin
steps.prompt: What does this person say?

steps.partnerSays: Freut mich. Ich heiße Lea. Woher kommen Sie?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Nice to meet you. My name is Lea. Where are you from?
steps.prompt: Say where you're from and return the question:
options: Ich komme aus den USA. Und Sie?
steps.correctAnswer: Ich komme aus den USA. Und Sie?
steps.explanation: "Ich komme aus den USA. Und Sie?" answers her question and keeps the conversation balanced.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: “Ich heiße Sam” means…
steps.explanation: Heißen = to be called.

steps.title: Check · origin
steps.prompt: Best line for “I come from Belgium”?
steps.explanation: Kommen aus + country expresses origin.

title: Colors & simple descriptions
description: Name colors and describe everyday objects.

steps.title: Painting with words
steps.body: Colors are adjectives and agree in gender, number, and case with the noun.

steps.title: Agreement basics
steps.body: In predicative position (after sein) colors stay uninflected. Attributive forms take endings.
bullets: Das Auto ist rot.
ein rotes Auto
Most beginners start with predicative forms.

steps.prompt: Match each German color with its English name:
Arrange the stones to say: "The sky is blue.":
steps.explanation: Color + polite form — everything needed to express a preference in any shop.

steps.title: Listen · color
steps.prompt: You hear “Der Himmel ist blau”. What is being described?
Say you'd like the red one:
steps.explanation: "Ich hätte gerne das Rote" names the color politely with ich hätte gerne.

steps.title: Check · predicative
steps.prompt: How do you say “The sky is blue”?
steps.explanation: Predicative adjectives stay uninflected after sein.

steps.title: Check · color
steps.prompt: What is “black” in German?
steps.explanation: Schwarz = black.

title: At the café
description: Order drinks and ask for the bill with confidence.

steps.title: A quiet table
steps.body: Learn a handful of drink words plus two key phrases — s'il vous plaît equivalents — and you can order confidently anywhere.

steps.title: Café culture
steps.body: In many countries, un café means a short espresso. Always clarify 'for here' or 'to go' when ordering.
bullets: Asking for the bill is an active request — servers rarely bring it unsolicited.
Tipping customs vary widely — research the local norm.

phrases.source: I would like a coffee, please.
phrases.target: Ich hätte gerne einen Kaffee, bitte.

phrases.source: Can I have some tap water?

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I would like a coffee, please.":
steps.targetSentence: Ich hätte gerne einen Kaffee, bitte.
steps.targetTranslation: I would like a coffee, please.
steps.explanation: A polite order that works in any café — commit it to memory for the first sip.

steps.title: Listen · Rechnung
steps.prompt: How do you ask for the bill?
Order a coffee politely:
steps.explanation: "Einen Kaffee, bitte" uses the accusative form of ein for masculine nouns.

steps.title: Check · bill
steps.prompt: How do you say "the bill" in German?
steps.explanation: Die Rechnung is the bill in German.

steps.title: Check · to go
steps.prompt: How do you say "to go" when ordering?
steps.explanation: Zum Mitnehmen literally means "for taking along".

title: At the market
description: Fruit, quantities, and polite requests at a stall.

steps.title: Market pace
steps.body: Markets reward clear numbers and a polite request word. Pointing plus a word works — language makes it smoother.

phrases.target: Ich hätte gerne drei Äpfel, bitte.

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I'd like three apples, please.":
steps.targetSentence: Ich hätte gerne drei Äpfel, bitte.
steps.explanation: Quantity, item, price question — the complete phrase for any market stall.

steps.title: Listen · Preis
steps.prompt: How do you ask "How much does it cost?"
Ask for three apples and the price:
steps.explanation: "Drei Äpfel. Was kostet das?" adds to your order and asks the price.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you ask for the price in German?
steps.explanation: Was kostet das? = How much does it cost? A core shopping phrase.

steps.title: Check · order
steps.prompt: Best for "three apples, please"?
steps.explanation: Drei Äpfel, bitte directly matches the request.

title: Small talk & weather
description: Light conversation beyond hello.

steps.title: Beyond hello
steps.body: Weather and weekend questions are safe bridges after greetings. A simple comment on the sun or rain opens doors.

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Nice weather today.":
steps.explanation: A light observation that opens the door to warm, easy conversation.

steps.title: Listen · Regen
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's raining"?
Agree and keep the chat going:
options: Ja, die Sonne scheint. Wie war Ihr Wochenende?
steps.correctAnswer: Ja, die Sonne scheint. Wie war Ihr Wochenende?
steps.explanation: Agreeing and asking about the weekend is classic small talk.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's raining" in German?
steps.explanation: Es regnet uses regnen (to rain) in the third person singular.

steps.title: Check · weekend
steps.prompt: How do you ask "How was your weekend?" formally?
steps.explanation: Wie war…? = How was…? Ihr is the formal your.

title: At the restaurant
description: Reservations, ordering a meal, and dietary needs.

steps.title: From table to bill
steps.body: A restaurant visit follows a clear rhythm: being seated, ordering, and eventually asking for the bill.

steps.title: Menu know-how
steps.body: In many European countries, il menù/el menú/die Speisekarte is the full list of dishes.
bullets: The starter may be called entrante, antipasto, or Vorspeise.
The main course: plato principal, secondo piatto, Hauptgericht.
Say Buen provecho / Buon appetito / Guten Appetit before eating.

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "A table for two, please.":
steps.explanation: The natural, confident way to place an order with any server.

steps.title: Listen · recommendation
steps.prompt: How do you ask "What do you recommend?"
Order the fish:
options: Ich steige an der nächsten Haltestelle aus.
steps.explanation: "Ich nehme…" is the standard way to order in a German restaurant.

steps.title: Check · Speisekarte
steps.prompt: Die Speisekarte refers to…
options: The full list of every dish
steps.explanation: Die Speisekarte is the full menu with all dishes listed.

steps.title: Check · vegetarian
steps.prompt: A woman says "I'm vegetarian." Which form does she use?
steps.explanation: Vegetarierin is the feminine form in German.

title: Talking about plans
description: Express what you're going to do using the near future.

steps.title: The near future
steps.body: Each language has a simple structure to talk about upcoming plans — usually involving "to go" or a future auxiliary plus an infinitive.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: Learn the subject + "going to/will" + infinitive pattern for your target language.
bullets: Spanish: ir a + infinitivo
German: werden + infinitive
Italian: future tense or andare a + infinito

phrases.source: What are you going to do this weekend?
I'm going to visit my parents.
We're going to watch a film.
She's going to travel to Berlin.

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I'm going to visit my parents.":
steps.targetTranslation: I'm going to visit my parents.
steps.explanation: Future marker + plan — two building blocks for any upcoming arrangement.

steps.title: Listen · structure
steps.prompt: Which sentence uses the German future tense correctly?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: What are you doing this weekend?
steps.prompt: Say you're going to visit your parents:
steps.explanation: "Ich werde…" + infinitive forms the future tense in German.

steps.title: Check · structure
steps.prompt: Which correctly uses werden + infinitive?
steps.explanation: Werden + infinitive: ich werde + essen (unconjugated).

steps.title: Check · translate
steps.prompt: How do you say "We will travel"?
steps.explanation: Wir werden + reisen = We will travel.

title: Simple directions
description: Left, right, straight — and asking where something is.

steps.title: Finding your way
steps.body: Combine "where is…?" with a few direction words for short walks in a new city.

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Go straight ahead, then left.":
steps.explanation: Left, right, and straight — three words that will get you anywhere in the city.

steps.title: Listen · where
steps.prompt: How do you ask "Where is the station?"

steps.partnerSays: Gehen Sie geradeaus, dann links. Es ist gegenüber der Apotheke.
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Go straight, then left. It's opposite the pharmacy.
steps.prompt: Ask whether it's far:
steps.explanation: "Ist es weit?" is the natural follow-up after getting directions.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you say "straight ahead" in German?
steps.explanation: Geradeaus means straight ahead — a key direction word.

steps.title: Check · ask
steps.prompt: How do you ask where the station is?
steps.explanation: Wo ist…? = Where is…? — the essential navigation question.

title: Travel phrases
description: Tickets, platforms, and delays.

steps.title: On the move
steps.body: Stations repeat the same patterns: destination, platform, delay, seat. Learn them once.

phrases.target: Eine Hin- und Rückfahrkarte nach Berlin.

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "A ticket to Munich, please.":
steps.explanation: A direct question that instantly tells you if you're running on schedule.

steps.title: Listen · delay
steps.prompt: How do you say "The train is delayed"?

steps.partnerSays: Der Zug fährt von Gleis drei ab.
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: The train leaves from platform three.
steps.prompt: Ask if the train is running late:
steps.explanation: "Hat der Zug Verspätung?" is the standard way to ask about a delay.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you say "a ticket" in German?
steps.explanation: Eine Fahrkarte is the ticket; das Gleis is the platform.

steps.title: Check · delay
steps.prompt: How do you say "delayed" in German?
steps.explanation: Mit Verspätung means with delay; pünktlich means on time.

title: At the hotel
description: Check-in lines and simple room requests.

steps.title: Front desk
steps.body: Reservation, nights, and room type cover most check-ins.

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I have a reservation.":
steps.explanation: A short statement that confirms your booking and sets check-in in motion.

steps.title: Listen · breakfast
steps.prompt: How do you ask "Is breakfast included?"
Confirm and ask about breakfast:
steps.explanation: "Ja. Ist das Frühstück inbegriffen?" confirms and asks a key check-in question.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you say "I have a reservation"?
steps.explanation: Haben (to have) + eine Reservierung = I have a reservation.

steps.title: Check · checkout
steps.prompt: How do you ask what time checkout is?
steps.explanation: Der Check-out is the standard term for checkout time in German hotels.

title: Getting around town
description: Buses, metro, taxis, and buying tickets.

steps.title: Moving through the city
steps.body: Most cities run on a mix of metro, bus, and tram. A few words cover most fare questions.

phrases.source: Does this bus go to the center?
I'm getting off at the next stop.
phrases.target: Ich steige an der nächsten Haltestelle aus.

phrases.source: Can you call me a taxi?
phrases.target: Können Sie mir ein Taxi rufen?

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Does this bus go to the center?":
steps.targetTranslation: Does this bus go to the center?
steps.explanation: The phrase that ends any bus or metro journey gracefully.

steps.title: Listen · aussteigen
steps.prompt: How do you say "I'm getting off here" on the U-Bahn?

steps.partnerSays: Ja, dieser Bus fährt ins Zentrum.
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Yes, this bus goes to the center.
steps.prompt: Say you're getting off at the next stop:
options: Ich steige an der nächsten Haltestelle aus.
steps.correctAnswer: Ich steige an der nächsten Haltestelle aus.
steps.explanation: "Ich steige … aus" uses the separable verb aussteigen.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: Eine Tageskarte usually refers to…
steps.explanation: Eine Tageskarte is a day pass; eine Einzelfahrkarte is a single fare.

steps.title: Check · getting off
steps.prompt: How do you say "I'm getting off here"?
steps.explanation: Aussteigen (to get off) is separable: aus goes to the end.

title: Pharmacy & feeling unwell
description: Describe symptoms and get help at a pharmacy.

steps.title: Green cross, calm help
steps.body: Pharmacies are trained to advise on minor issues before you need a doctor.

steps.title: Pain pattern
steps.body: The pattern for expressing pain: "I have pain in (body part)."
bullets: Spanish: me duele la cabeza
German: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen
Italian: Ho mal di testa

phrases.source: Do you have something for a sore throat?

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I have a headache.":
steps.explanation: Describing the most common ache — clear and calm gets you the right remedy.

steps.title: Listen · Bauch
steps.prompt: Which phrase means "I have a stomach ache"?
Say no and ask for something for your throat:
options: Nein. Haben Sie etwas für den Hals?
steps.correctAnswer: Nein. Haben Sie etwas für den Hals?
steps.explanation: "Nein. Haben Sie etwas für den Hals?" answers and asks for an over-the-counter remedy.

steps.title: Check · pattern
steps.prompt: How do you say "I have a headache" in German?
steps.explanation: Kopfschmerzen (headache) is a compound noun. Ich habe Kopfschmerzen = I have a headache.

steps.title: Check · emergency
steps.prompt: Which phrase calls for urgent help?
steps.explanation: Hilfe! is the standard exclamation for calling for help in German.

title: Telling time
description: Ask for and give the time, on the hour and beyond.

steps.title: What time is it?
steps.body: Each language has a key question for asking the time and a standard way to give it.

steps.title: Minute expressions
steps.body: Learn these fixed chunks rather than translating word for word.
bullets: Spanish: y cuarto (quarter past), y media (half past), menos cuarto (quarter to)
German: Viertel nach (quarter past), halb (half), Viertel vor (quarter to)
Italian: e un quarto (quarter past), e mezza (half past), meno un quarto (quarter to)

phrases.target: Der Zug fährt um 14:30 Uhr ab.

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "It's half past seven.":
steps.explanation: Hour + "half" — the most common time expression in everyday conversation.

steps.title: Listen · quarter to
steps.prompt: How do you say "quarter to nine" in German?
Thank her and say when your train leaves:
options: Danke. Der Zug fährt um drei Uhr ab.
Entschuldigung, wie viel Uhr ist es?
steps.correctAnswer: Danke. Der Zug fährt um drei Uhr ab.
steps.explanation: "Danke. Der Zug fährt um drei Uhr ab" thanks her and states the departure time.

steps.title: Check · halb
steps.prompt: "Halb acht" in German means…
steps.explanation: Halb acht means "half to eight" = 7:30. German counts toward the next hour.

steps.title: Check · noon
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's noon" in German?
steps.explanation: Mittag is noon (midday); Mitternacht is midnight.

title: Days, months & dates
description: The calendar and how to say a date.

steps.title: The week starts on Monday
steps.body: Romance language calendars typically start the week with Monday. Days and months are NOT capitalized.

steps.title: Saying a date
steps.body: Romance languages use day + month (no ordinals except "1st"). German uses ordinal numbers.
bullets: Spanish: el primero de mayo = May 1st
German: der erste Mai = May 1st
Italian: il primo maggio = May 1st
Days and months are lowercase in Spanish and Italian, capitalized in German.

phrases.target: Mein Geburtstag ist der erste Mai.

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "My birthday is May 1st.":
steps.targetSentence: Mein Geburtstag ist der erste Mai.
steps.explanation: A date in full — once you know the pattern, every date falls into place.

steps.title: Listen · day
steps.prompt: How do you say "Today is Monday" in German?
Say it's Wednesday:
steps.explanation: "Heute ist Mittwoch" answers with the day. Days are capitalized in German.

steps.title: Check · order
steps.prompt: Which day comes right after Mittwoch?
steps.explanation: The order is Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag, Freitag, Samstag, Sonntag.

steps.title: Check · capitalization
steps.prompt: In German, days and months are…
steps.explanation: All nouns in German are capitalized, including days (Montag) and months (Januar).

title: Talking about family
description: Name family members and describe relationships.

steps.title: Who's who
steps.body: Family vocabulary combines nicely with "to have" and possessive adjectives.

steps.title: Possessives
steps.body: Possessives agree with the noun that follows, not the owner's gender.
bullets: Spanish: mi hermano (my brother), mi hermana (my sister)
German: mein Bruder, meine Schwester
Italian: mio fratello, mia sorella

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I have two brothers.":
steps.explanation: A warm, simple statement that naturally invites the other person to share too.

steps.title: Listen · possessive
steps.prompt: How do you say "my sister" in German?

steps.partnerSays: Schön, Sie kennenzulernen. Haben Sie Geschwister?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Nice to meet you. Do you have siblings?
steps.prompt: Say you have two brothers:
steps.explanation: "Ja, ich habe zwei Brüder" answers directly using haben.

steps.title: Check · possessive
steps.prompt: How do you say "my sister" in German?
steps.explanation: Schwester is feminine → meine Schwester.

steps.title: Check · plural
steps.prompt: How do you say "my parents" in German?
steps.explanation: Eltern is plural → meine Eltern (nominative plural).

title: Shopping for clothes
description: Sizes, trying things on, and asking about price.

steps.title: Trying it on
steps.body: Clothes shopping mixes size, color, and a few polite requests to try things on or ask for a different size.

phrases.source: Do you have this in a size 40?
phrases.target: Haben Sie das in Größe vierzig?

phrases.source: Do you have a bigger size?

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Do you have this in a size 40?":
steps.targetSentence: Haben Sie das in Größe vierzig?
steps.targetTranslation: Do you have this in a size 40?
steps.explanation: The one question that keeps a shopping trip moving in the right direction.

steps.title: Listen · size
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's too small"?

steps.partnerSays: Natürlich. Die Umkleidekabine ist dort drüben.
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Of course. The fitting room is over there.
steps.prompt: After trying it on, say it's too small and ask for a bigger size:
options: Es ist zu klein. Haben Sie eine größere Größe?
steps.correctAnswer: Es ist zu klein. Haben Sie eine größere Größe?
steps.explanation: "Es ist zu klein. Haben Sie eine größere Größe?" describes the problem and asks for the next size.

steps.title: Check · size
steps.prompt: How do you ask "do you have this in a size 40?"
options: Haben Sie das in Größe vierzig?
steps.explanation: Größe means size; Größe vierzig = size 40.

steps.title: Check · too small
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's too small"?
steps.explanation: Zu klein = too small; zu groß = too big.

title: Articles & gender
description: Noun gender and the articles that show it.

steps.title: Every noun has a gender
steps.body: In Romance languages, nouns are masculine or feminine. In German, there are three genders. Articles show that gender. Memorize nouns with their article.

steps.title: Learning habit
steps.body: Don't just learn 'house'. Learn 'the house' with its article. The article is part of the word.
bullets: Spanish: el/la (the), un/una (a)
German: der/die/das (the), ein/eine/ein (a)
Italian: il/la (the), un/una (a), lo/gli for special cases

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "the table":
steps.explanation: A compact phrase that puts the article or gender rule into immediate practice.

steps.title: Listen · gender
steps.prompt: Which article fits with "Frau" (woman)?
steps.explanation: Frau is feminine → die / eine Frau.

steps.partnerSays: Wie sagt man "the table" auf Deutsch?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: How do you say "the table" in German?
steps.prompt: Answer with the correct article:
steps.explanation: Tisch is masculine in German, so it takes der (nominative).

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: Which article fits with "Kind" (child) in German?
steps.explanation: Kind is neuter in German → das Kind / ein Kind.

steps.title: Check · plural
steps.prompt: The plural definite article for all genders in German is…
steps.explanation: Die is used for all plural nouns regardless of gender.

steps.title: Check · feminine
steps.prompt: Which article fits with "Frau" (woman) in German?
steps.explanation: Frau is feminine → die Frau / eine Frau.

title: To be & to have
description: The two verbs you'll use every day.

steps.title: Workhorses
steps.body: The verbs "to be" and "to have" appear constantly in descriptions, states, and idioms.

phrases.note: Idiom: Hunger haben = to be hungry

steps.prompt: Match each German word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I am tired.":
steps.explanation: Two core verbs in a single sentence — a powerful combination to internalize.

steps.title: Listen · idiom
steps.prompt: How do you say "They are hungry"?
Say you're tired and hungry:
options: Ich bin müde und ich habe Hunger.
Ich habe müde und ich bin Hunger.
Ich bin Hunger und ich habe müde.
steps.correctAnswer: Ich bin müde und ich habe Hunger.
steps.explanation: Müde uses sein (ich bin müde), while Hunger uses haben (ich habe Hunger).

steps.title: Check · sein
steps.prompt: How do you say "I am"?
steps.explanation: Ich bin comes from sein (to be).

steps.title: Check · haben
steps.prompt: "Ich habe eine Reservierung" uses…
steps.explanation: Ich habe comes from haben (to have).

steps.title: Check · idiom
steps.prompt: How do you say "they are hungry" in German?
steps.explanation: Hunger haben is the idiom — German uses "have" where English uses "be" for hunger.

title: Regular verbs
description: Conjugate the most common verb family.

steps.title: The biggest group
steps.body: Most verbs in these languages follow a regular pattern — learn it once, apply it to hundreds of verbs.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body: Drop the infinitive ending, add the personal ending for each subject.
bullets: Spanish -ar: habl-ar → hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan
German regular: spiel-en → spiele, spielst, spielt, spielen, spielt, spielen
Italian -are: parl-are → parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano

steps.title: Listen · wir form
steps.prompt: Which form is correct for "we work"?
Say yes, you speak a little German:
options: Ja, ich spreche ein bisschen Deutsch.
Ja, ich sprichst ein bisschen Deutsch.
Ja, ich sprechen ein bisschen Deutsch.
steps.correctAnswer: Ja, ich spreche ein bisschen Deutsch.
steps.explanation: With ich, sprechen takes -e: ich spreche.

steps.title: Check · ending
steps.prompt: What ending goes with du for regular verbs?
steps.explanation: Du takes -st: du spielst, du lernst, du kaufst.

steps.title: Check · sie/wir
steps.prompt: What ending goes with wir for regular verbs?
steps.explanation: Wir takes -en: wir spielen, wir arbeiten.

title: Adjective agreement
description: Make descriptive words match the noun they describe.

steps.title: Adjectives match their nouns
steps.body: In Romance languages, adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number. In German, predicate adjectives (after 'to be') stay unchanged.

steps.title: The default rule
steps.body: Add -a/-e for feminine, -s for plural in Romance languages. German predicate adjectives don't decline.
bullets: Spanish: gran-d → grande (m/f), grand-es (pl)
German: Er ist groß / Sie ist groß (no change after sein)
Italian: grand-e → grande (m/f), grand-i (pl)

title: Saying no
description: Turn any sentence negative with simple patterns.

steps.title: Negation patterns
steps.body: Each language has a characteristic way to negate a verb. Learn the pattern, apply it everywhere.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: The position of 'no/nicht/non' differs in each language.
bullets: Spanish: no before the verb. Double negation is standard: no veo nada.
German: nicht usually late in the sentence; kein negates nouns.
Italian: non before the verb. Double negation standard: non vedo niente.

steps.title: Check · nicht vs. kein
steps.prompt: Which sentence correctly negates a noun (Kaffee)?
steps.explanation: Kein/keine negates nouns; nicht negates verbs and adjectives.

steps.title: Check · position
steps.prompt: Where does "nicht" usually go in a German sentence?
options: Usually toward the end, after the verb's complement
steps.explanation: Nicht typically comes after the object or complement, before a predicate adjective or infinitive.

title: Asking questions
description: Question words and patterns.

steps.title: Asking around
steps.body: Each language has its own set of question words and question-formation patterns.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Yes/no questions and information questions each have their own structure.
bullets: Spanish: rise in intonation + ¿…? punctuation. Or inversion (¿Habla usted inglés?).
German: Verb first for yes/no (Sprichst du Deutsch?). W-word + verb for info questions.
Italian: Intonation (rise) for yes/no. Question word + normal word order for info questions.
